effects.title: Acoustic emission
effects.effect: a material under strain clicks with tiny bursts of sound as cracks grow
effects.description: A metal or rock under growing strain gives off tiny bursts of sound each time a crack jumps forward or a grain slips, like the 'cry' a bar of tin makes when bent. Joseph Kaiser studied it systematically in 1950, and now sensors stuck to tanks, bridges and aircraft listen for cracks before they become failures.
usedIn: Crack monitoring of pressure vessels and storage tanks
Bridge and aircraft-wing structural health monitoring
effects.strength: The clicks are far too faint and high-pitched to hear, but a sensor glued to a steel tank can pick up a crack growing a fraction of a millimetre several metres away.

effects.title: Acoustic radiation pressure
effects.effect: a strong sound wave pushes steadily on objects and can float them in mid-air
effects.description: A strong sound wave pushes steadily on whatever it hits, and in a standing wave small beads or droplets get trapped and float in mid-air at the quiet spots. Lord Rayleigh worked out the push in 1902; today it levitates samples in labs, sorts cells on chips and lets you feel buttons in mid-air.
usedIn: Acoustic levitators for containerless lab chemistry
Acoustic tweezers that sort blood cells on a chip
effects.strength: Weak: ultrasound can float droplets and foam beads a few millimetres across, but the force is only a few thousandths of a newton.

effects.title: Acousto-optic effect
effects.effect: a sound wave in a crystal bends and shifts a light beam passing through
effects.description: A sound wave running through a clear crystal makes ripples of squeezed and stretched material that bend a light beam like a grating; change the sound's pitch and the beam swings to a new angle. Léon Brillouin predicted it in 1922, and it now switches and steers laser beams with no moving parts.
usedIn: Acousto-optic modulators in laser printers and laser engravers
Brillouin fibre sensors that measure strain along kilometres of pipeline
effects.strength: An ultrasound wave in a crystal can redirect most of a laser beam in under a microsecond, millions of times faster than a moving mirror.

effects.title: Adiabatic heating and cooling
effects.effect: a gas heats up when quickly squeezed and cools when it quickly expands
effects.description: Squeeze air quickly and it gets hot; let it expand quickly and it gets cold, even with no heat going in or out. Erasmus Darwin described air chilling as it rushed out of an air gun in 1788. Squeezing ignites fuel in diesel engines, and expanding air cools airliner cabins and makes clouds.
effects.strength: Squeezing air to a twentieth of its volume, as a diesel engine does, heats it above 500 °C, hot enough to light fuel with no spark.

effects.title: Adsorption
effects.effect: molecules from a gas or liquid stick to the surface of a solid
effects.description: Gas or dissolved molecules stick to the surface of a solid in a thin film, so a porous solid like charcoal soaks up huge amounts. Carl Scheele noticed charcoal taking up gases in 1773, and Felice Fontana saw the same in 1777. It's how gas masks, water-filter jugs and the silica-gel packets in shoe boxes work.
effects.strength: A single gram of activated charcoal has the inner surface area of a few tennis courts, enough to soak up a large share of its own weight in vapour.

effects.title: Auger effect
effects.effect: an atom that loses an inner electron throws out a second electron with a telltale energy
effects.description: When an atom loses an inner electron, it can fill the gap by flinging out a second electron with an energy that is a fingerprint of the element. Pierre Auger saw the tracks in a cloud chamber in 1923. Measuring these electrons tells which atoms sit on a surface, which is how chipmakers check wafers for contamination.
usedIn: Auger electron spectroscopy for checking chip and metal surfaces
Surface analysis of catalysts and corrosion films
effects.strength: The electrons only escape from the top few layers of atoms, so it reads a surface less than a hundred-thousandth of a hair's width deep; it needs a vacuum chamber and an electron beam.

effects.title: Auxetic effect
effects.effect: a material gets fatter when stretched and thinner when squeezed
effects.description: Stretch most things and they get thinner; an auxetic material gets fatter instead, and squeezing it makes it shrink in every direction. Roderic Lakes made the first auxetic foam in 1987 by crushing ordinary foam so its cells buckled inward. It makes padding that firms up where it's hit and stents that open evenly.
usedIn: Impact padding in helmets and body armour
Shoe soles that widen as the foot pushes off (Nike Free RN, 2016)
effects.strength: Lakes's foam widened by about seven-tenths of how much it lengthened, where a rubber band narrows by about half.

effects.title: Avalanche breakdown
effects.effect: one fast electron knocks loose others in a cascade that suddenly lets current flow
effects.description: In a strong enough electric field, one free electron speeds up, smashes loose another, and those two free two more, until a flood of current pours through a gas or crystal that normally blocks it. John Townsend explained the cascade in gases around 1901. It makes Geiger counters click and lets light sensors catch single photons.
usedIn: Avalanche photodiodes in lidar and fibre-optic receivers
effects.strength: One electron can multiply into millions in under a microsecond, enough to turn a single particle or photon into a pulse you can count.

effects.title: Barkhausen effect
effects.effect: a magnetised piece of iron crackles as tiny regions inside it flip one by one
effects.description: Magnetise a piece of iron slowly and it doesn't change smoothly: tiny regions flip one after another, and a coil wound round it hears them as a crackle in a loudspeaker. Heinrich Barkhausen heard it in 1919. Factories now use the crackle to spot stress and grinding burns in gears and crankshafts.
usedIn: Barkhausen-noise inspection of gears, camshafts and bearings
Measuring stress in steel rails and pipes
effects.strength: The crackle is faint, heard only through a sensitive coil and amplifier, but it reads stress in the top tenth of a millimetre of steel.

effects.title: Bingham plastic
effects.effect: a paste stays solid until pushed past a threshold, then flows
effects.description: Some pastes act like a solid until you push hard enough, then flow like a liquid: toothpaste sits in a stripe on the brush but squirts out of the tube. Eugene Bingham described the behaviour in 1916 while studying paints. It's why paint doesn't drip and why drilling mud holds rock chips up when the pump stops.
usedIn: Drilling mud that suspends rock cuttings
effects.strength: Toothpaste holds a stripe a centimetre tall without slumping, yet a gentle squeeze is enough to make it flow.

effects.title: Bioluminescence
effects.effect: a living thing makes light by a chemical reaction in its body
effects.description: Fireflies, glowing mushrooms and deep-sea fish make their own light by a chemical reaction in their bodies, with almost no heat. Raphaël Dubois showed in 1885 that it takes two substances, which he named luciferin and luciferase. Firefly chemistry now lights up food-safety tests and shows biologists which genes are switched on.
usedIn: ATP hygiene swabs in food factories and hospitals
Luciferase reporter genes in biology labs
effects.strength: Dim: a jar of fireflies barely lets you read, but almost all the reaction's energy comes out as light rather than heat.

effects.title: Brazil nut effect
effects.effect: shaking a mix of grains brings the biggest pieces to the top
effects.description: Shake a jar of mixed nuts and the big Brazil nuts rise to the top, even though they're heavier. Anthony Rosato and colleagues named and simulated it in 1987: small pieces slip into the gaps under big ones, ratcheting them upward. It sorts gravel and grain, and it's why mixed powders unmix on a bumpy truck ride.
usedIn: Vibrating screens that sort gravel and seed by size
effects.strength: A few minutes of shaking is enough to bring a large nut from the bottom of a jar to the top.

effects.title: Capillary condensation
effects.effect: water vapour condenses inside tiny pores before the air is saturated
effects.description: In very narrow pores, water vapour turns to liquid even when the air isn't humid enough to make dew anywhere else, because the curved surface in the pore holds it more easily. Lord Kelvin worked out the rule in 1871. It helps drying packets pull moisture from air, makes powders clump on damp days and lets labs measure pore sizes.
usedIn: Gas-sorption instruments that measure pore sizes in catalysts
effects.strength: In a pore a few millionths of a millimetre wide, water condenses at about half the humidity needed for dew in open air.

effects.title: Cavitation
effects.effect: low pressure in a fast or shaken liquid makes bubbles that collapse violently
effects.description: Where a liquid moves fast or is shaken hard, its pressure drops so low that vapour bubbles appear, then collapse violently. Charles Parsons found in 1894 that this was what stopped his turbine ship Turbinia's propellers from gripping the water, and why they pitted. The same collapsing bubbles scrub jewellery clean in ultrasonic baths.
effects.strength: Each collapsing bubble briefly reaches thousands of atmospheres, enough to pit a bronze propeller over weeks.

effects.title: Centrifugal force
effects.effect: a spinning object presses outward, harder the faster it spins
effects.description: Anything going round in a circle seems flung outward, pressing harder the faster it spins: water stays in a bucket swung overhead. Christiaan Huygens worked out its size in 1659. Spin it fast enough and it squeezes water from clothes, cream from milk and heavy particles from light ones.
effects.strength: A washing machine spinning at 1,200 rpm presses the clothes against the drum with about 400 times their weight.

effects.title: Cheerio effect
effects.effect: small floating objects drift together because of the dents they make in the surface
effects.description: Cereal floating in milk clumps together and sticks to the bowl's edge, because each piece dents the liquid surface and the dents slide into each other. Dominic Vella and L. Mahadevan explained and named it in 2005. It can pull small floating parts together into ordered patterns without any hands.
usedIn: Bragg and Nye's bubble rafts that model crystal defects
effects.strength: Weak and short-range: it only pulls floating objects a few millimetres across, over a few centimetres, in a few seconds.

effects.title: Christiansen effect
effects.effect: crushed glass in a liquid lets through only the one colour where both bend light equally
effects.description: A glass cell packed with crushed glass and a liquid looks milky, except for one colour that passes straight through: the one where glass and liquid bend light by exactly the same amount. Christian Christiansen found it in 1884. Warming the cell shifts which colour gets through, so it makes simple tunable colour filters.
usedIn: Narrow-band Christiansen filters for light and infrared
effects.strength: A cell a few centimetres thick passes a band of light only a few nanometres wide, and warming it by a few degrees shifts the colour noticeably.

effects.title: Coanda effect
effects.effect: a jet of fluid clings to a curved surface beside it and follows its curve
effects.description: A jet of air or water bends to follow a curved surface beside it instead of shooting straight: hold the back of a spoon under a tap and the stream wraps around it. Henri Coandă noticed it in 1910 when exhaust from his experimental jet aircraft hugged its body. It's how bladeless fans blow and some helicopters steer without a tail rotor.
usedIn: NOTAR helicopters with no tail rotor
Blown wing flaps on short-takeoff planes (Antonov An-72)
effects.strength: A thin jet can be bent through 90 degrees or more around a rounded edge, dragging along several times its own volume of surrounding air.

effects.title: Coffee ring effect
effects.effect: a drying drop carries its particles to its edge and leaves a ring
effects.description: A drop of coffee dries into a dark ring rather than an even spot, because liquid flows outward to replace what evaporates fastest at the edge and carries the grounds with it. Robert Deegan and colleagues explained it in 1997. Printers fight it to get even ink, and some cheap medical tests use it to sort particles by size.
usedIn: Inkjet printing of electronics (suppressed or exploited for thin conductive rings)
Paper diagnostics that separate particles by size
effects.strength: Within a few minutes a drying drop sweeps nearly all its particles to the rim.

effects.title: Corona discharge
effects.effect: air around a sharp high-voltage point glows and becomes charged without sparking
effects.description: Around a sharp point or thin wire at high voltage, the air starts to glow faintly blue and hiss as it becomes electrically charged, without a spark jumping. Sailors called it St Elmo's fire; Frank Peek worked out when it starts in 1915. It charges the drum in photocopiers, cleans soot from chimney smoke and makes ozone.
usedIn: Charging the drum in photocopiers and laser printers
effects.strength: A few thousand volts on a needle point is enough to start it, and a precipitator built on it catches over 99% of the ash in smoke.

effects.title: Detonation
effects.effect: a burning front driven by its own shock wave races through an explosive faster than sound
effects.description: In some explosives the burning doesn't spread layer by layer like a fire; it rides a shock wave that tears through the material faster than sound, crushing as it goes. Berthelot and Vieille in Paris measured these flame fronts in gas-filled tubes in 1881. It's why dynamite shatters rock while gunpowder only pushes, and it lets welders bang dissimilar metals together into one plate.
usedIn: Explosive welding of steel to titanium or copper cladding
Shaped-charge perforators that punch oil wells
Rotating detonation rocket engines (test-fired in the 2020s)
effects.strength: The front moves at 2 to 9 km per second with pressures of a few hundred thousand atmospheres, enough to shatter steel on contact.

effects.title: Diamagnetism
effects.effect: a material is weakly pushed away from a magnet instead of pulled toward it
effects.description: Water, wood, graphite and even living things are weakly pushed away by a strong magnet, the opposite of iron. Faraday showed in 1845 that most substances do this (Brugmans had seen bismuth do it in 1778). With a strong enough magnet it can float a frog in mid-air, or a sliver of graphite over a row of fridge-size magnets with no power at all.
usedIn: Levitating a live frog in a 16-tesla magnet (Geim and Berry, 1997)
Floating pyrolytic-graphite desk toys and levitation stages
Diamagnetic bearings and sensors in micro-machines
effects.strength: About a hundred-thousandth the strength of iron's pull: a thin sheet of pyrolytic graphite floats a millimetre above neodymium magnets, but floating water takes a magnetic field about 300,000 times Earth's.

effects.title: Dielectric heating
effects.effect: radio waves or microwaves shake molecules in a material and heat it from the inside
effects.description: Radio waves or microwaves make water and other polar molecules in food flip back and forth billions of times a second, and the jostling heats the food from inside. Percy Spencer at Raytheon noticed a chocolate bar melting in his pocket next to a radar magnetron in 1945 and built the first microwave oven. The same trick welds plastic sheets and dries timber.
usedIn: Radio-frequency welding of PVC (inflatable boats, blister packs)
Drying timber and curing glue in plywood presses
effects.strength: A 1,000-watt microwave oven brings a mug of water to the boil in about two minutes.

effects.title: Diffusiophoresis
effects.effect: particles in a liquid drift along a difference in dissolved-salt concentration
effects.description: Tiny particles in a liquid drift on their own toward or away from places where dissolved salt or sugar is more concentrated, with no current or stirring. Boris Derjaguin in Moscow described it in 1947 while studying how latex particles coat surfaces. It pulls dirt out of pores too small for any rinse to reach and sorts particles in lab-on-a-chip devices.
usedIn: Latex coating in dip-moulded gloves and balloons
Pulling dirt out of fabric and porous surfaces with salt gradients (lab-tested)
effects.strength: Slow, a few micrometres per second, but enough to empty a pore a hair's width deep in under a minute.

effects.title: Brewster's angle
effects.effect: light glancing off glass or water at one angle comes off fully polarised
effects.description: Look at a lake at a shallow angle and the glare is light vibrating in one direction only; at one exact angle, about 53 degrees from straight down for water, it is completely so. David Brewster found the rule for that angle in 1815. It goes on the deck's Polarized light card as a second effect.
usedIn: Polarising sunglasses that cut glare off water and roads
Brewster windows that let laser light leave a tube without loss
effects.strength: At the angle, 100% of the reflected light is polarised; nearby angles still give most of the effect.

effects.title: Garshelis effect
effects.effect: twisting a magnetised shaft makes it give off a magnetic field
effects.description: Magnetise a ring on a steel shaft around its circumference and nothing leaks out, but twist the shaft and a measurable field appears along it, growing with the twist. Ivan Garshelis turned this into a way to weigh the turning force on a spinning shaft without touching it.
usedIn: Torque sensors in electric power steering
effects.strength: A few gauss at full torque, weak but easily read by a nearby Hall sensor.

effects.title: Magnetic saturation
effects.effect: iron can only be magnetised so far, then extra current adds almost nothing
effects.description: Push more current through a coil around iron and the iron's magnetism grows, until every tiny magnetic region in it is lined up; after that it barely grows at all. Henry Rowland measured this ceiling in 1873. Switching iron in and out of saturation lets a small current control a large one.
usedIn: Fluxgate magnetometers in spacecraft and phones
effects.strength: Iron saturates at about 2 tesla, some 40,000 times Earth's magnetic field.

effects.title: Eddy currents
effects.effect: a moving or changing magnetic field stirs up swirling currents in metal that brake it and heat it
effects.description: Move a magnet past a sheet of copper or aluminium and swirling currents spring up in the metal, dragging against the motion and warming it. Foucault showed in 1855 that a copper disc spun between magnet poles slows down and heats up. A magnet dropped down a copper pipe drifts down slowly as if through syrup, and the same drag stops trains and sorts drink cans.
usedIn: Eddy-current brakes on trains and roller coasters
Metal detectors and coin checkers in vending machines
Recycling separators that fling aluminium cans off a conveyor
effects.strength: A strong magnet takes several seconds to fall through a 30 cm copper pipe instead of a quarter of a second.

effects.title: Electret
effects.effect: a material holds a permanent electric charge, like an electric version of a magnet
effects.description: Some waxes and plastics, melted and left to harden inside a strong electric field, keep a frozen-in charge for years, an electric version of a permanent magnet. Mototaro Eguchi made the first from carnauba wax and resin in Tokyo in 1919. Thin charged plastic films now sit in almost every phone microphone, and the fibres of N95 masks are electrets that grab passing particles.
usedIn: Electret microphones in phones and hearing aids (Sessler and West, 1962)
Electrostatic air filters for heating and ventilation
effects.strength: A film thinner than paper can hold a few hundred volts on its surface for decades, enough to tug dust and smoke particles out of the air.

effects.title: Electric arc
effects.effect: a large current jumping a gap turns the air into a continuous, intensely hot glowing plasma
effects.description: Pull two touching carbon rods a little apart while a big current flows and a blinding, roaring bridge of hot glowing gas forms between them. Vasily Petrov in St Petersburg described it in 1802 using a huge battery, and Humphry Davy made it famous in London a few years later. Arcs lit the first street lamps and searchlights, and today they weld ships and melt scrap into new steel.
usedIn: Electric arc furnaces that recycle scrap steel
Arc lamps for searchlights and early cinema projectors
effects.strength: A welding arc reaches about 6,000 °C, hot enough to melt any metal in seconds.

effects.title: Electric wind
effects.effect: a sharp point at high voltage blows a breeze
effects.description: Air near a sharp point at high voltage becomes charged and is pushed away, making a breeze with no moving parts. It runs silent air purifiers, and in 2018 it flew a model plane with no propeller.
effects.strength: Yes, weak: the MIT plane weighed about 2.5 kg and flew just 60 m on a few newtons of thrust. Good for moving air quietly, not for lifting much.

effects.title: Electro-osmosis
effects.effect: a voltage across a wet porous material or narrow channel makes the liquid flow
effects.description: Put a voltage across wet clay or a hair-thin glass tube of water and the water itself starts to flow toward one electrode, with no pump and no moving parts. Ferdinand Reuss saw water climb through sand in Moscow in 1807, in the same experiments where he found clay particles moving the other way. Engineers use it to drain soggy soil, and lab-on-a-chip devices use it to pump tiny drops.
usedIn: Draining clay soil for excavations and embankments (Casagrande, 1930s)
Pumps in lab-on-a-chip and microfluidic devices
Liquid flow in capillary electrophoresis DNA sequencers
effects.strength: Slow but steady: around a millimetre per second through a hair-thin channel at a few hundred volts per centimetre.

effects.title: Electroabsorption
effects.effect: an electric field makes a semiconductor absorb light it used to let through
effects.description: A thin layer of semiconductor that normally lets a laser beam through starts to swallow it when a few volts are applied across it. Walter Franz in Germany and Leonid Keldysh in Moscow predicted it independently in 1958. Because it switches in trillionths of a second, it is used to flick laser light on and off to send internet data down optical fibres.
effects.strength: A couple of volts can block most of a beam, and it switches tens of billions of times a second.

effects.title: Electrocaloric effect
effects.effect: a material warms when an electric field is switched on and cools when it is switched off
effects.description: Some crystals and plastics warm up when you switch on a strong electric field across them and cool down when you switch it off. Kobeko and Kurchatov first measured it in Rochelle salt in Leningrad in 1930. Cycling a material this way can pump heat like a fridge with no gas and no compressor, and prototype solid-state coolers now do it.
usedIn: Prototype solid-state refrigerators using polymer films
effects.strength: Ordinary crystals change by a fraction of a degree, but thin films found in 2006 swing by about 12 °C per switch.

effects.title: Electrocapillarity
effects.effect: a voltage makes a drop spread out or bead up
effects.description: A voltage changes how well a liquid wets a surface: a drop of mercury in acid flattens or bulges as the voltage is turned up and down. Today it pushes droplets around lab chips and focuses liquid lenses.
usedIn: Lippmann's capillary electrometer, which recorded the first human heartbeat traces (1887)
Liquid lenses that focus by reshaping a drop
Lab-on-a-chip devices that move single drops around
effects.strength: Strong only at small sizes: it reshapes and moves drops a few millimetres across in thousandths of a second, but can't lift anything heavy.

effects.title: Electrochemiluminescence
effects.effect: an electrode reaction makes a chemical glow
effects.description: Certain chemicals glow when a small voltage at an electrode sets off a light-giving reaction, so the light can be switched on exactly when and where you want it. Chemists worked it out in the 1960s. It is the heart of hospital blood analysers that count tiny amounts of hormones, cancer markers and heart-attack proteins.
usedIn: Roche Elecsys immunoassay analysers (thyroid, cancer marker and troponin tests)
effects.strength: The glow is too faint to see, but a light detector can count it down to a few billionths of a gram per litre.

effects.title: Electrochromism
effects.effect: a small voltage makes a material change colour or darken, and it reverses
effects.description: A thin film on glass turns from clear to deep blue when a small voltage pushes charged atoms into it, and clears again when the voltage reverses. Satyen Deb found it in tungsten oxide films at American Cyanamid in 1969. It makes windows that dim at the press of a button and car mirrors that darken against headlight glare.
usedIn: Dimmable cabin windows on the Boeing 787
effects.strength: A couple of volts darkens a window over a few minutes, cutting the light let through from about 60% to 1%.

effects.title: Electron spin resonance
effects.effect: unpaired electrons in a magnetic field absorb microwaves at one precise frequency
effects.description: Put a substance with lone, unpaired electrons in a magnetic field and it soaks up microwaves at one sharp frequency, set by the field strength. Yevgeny Zavoisky found it in Kazan in 1944. Because it picks out free radicals and radiation damage, it can date fossil teeth, check whether food was irradiated, and measure radiation doses.
usedIn: Alanine dosimeters that measure radiotherapy doses
Testing whether food has been irradiated
effects.strength: Weak: it needs a sensitive microwave receiver, but it can spot about a billion unpaired electrons in a sample.

effects.title: Electrorheological effect
effects.effect: an electric field turns a fluid thick and nearly solid in milliseconds
effects.description: A runny oil full of fine powder stiffens into a soft solid in a few thousandths of a second when a strong voltage is applied, and turns runny again when it is switched off. Willis Winslow patented it in 1947. It gives clutches, brakes and haptic controls that change grip instantly with no moving valves.
usedIn: Adaptive shock absorbers and robot grippers
effects.strength: A few thousand volts per millimetre makes it hold a few kilopascals, roughly like stiff jelly, which is why magnetic versions won in car suspensions.

effects.title: Electrostatic induction
effects.effect: a nearby charge pushes the charges in an object around without touching it
effects.description: Hold a charged rod near a metal can without touching it and the can's own charges shift, so the near side becomes opposite to the rod and the can rolls toward it. John Canton in London described it in 1753. Touching the far side briefly lets you charge things over and over from one source, which is how the electrophorus and the Wimshurst machine work.
effects.strength: A rod rubbed on hair can pull an empty drink can along a table from a few centimetres away.

effects.title: Electrostriction
effects.effect: an insulator changes shape a little when an electric field is applied
effects.description: Every insulating material squeezes slightly in the direction of a strong electric field, and the effect doesn't care which way the field points. In most materials the change is far too small to notice, but special ceramics move enough to bend mirrors. Telescope mirrors that correct for starlight twinkling and precision positioners use these ceramics.
usedIn: Lead magnesium niobate actuators in adaptive-optics mirrors
effects.strength: Tiny: the best ceramics stretch about 0.1%, a millimetre-thick piece moving a micrometre.

effects.title: Faraday effect
effects.effect: a magnetic field twists the polarisation of light passing through a material
effects.description: Shine polarised light through glass sitting in a strong magnetic field and the direction of its polarisation twists, more the stronger the field. Faraday found it in 1845, the first proof that light and magnetism are linked. It builds one-way valves for light that protect lasers in fibre-optic networks, and lets power companies measure huge currents with a loop of fibre.
usedIn: Optical isolators in fibre-optic networks and lasers
Fibre-optic current sensors in power substations
Mapping galactic magnetic fields with radio telescopes
effects.strength: In special garnet crystals a small permanent magnet twists light by 45 degrees in a couple of millimetres; ordinary glass needs a strong electromagnet for a few degrees.

effects.title: Faraday waves
effects.effect: vibrating a container makes its liquid surface form standing wave patterns that can throw off droplets
effects.description: Shake a dish of liquid up and down fast enough and its surface breaks into a standing pattern of squares, stripes or hexagons that bob at half the shaking rate. Faraday described them in 1831. Shake much faster and the crests fling off fine droplets, which is how ultrasonic humidifiers and nebulisers make mist.
usedIn: Arranging cells and particles into patterns for tissue engineering
effects.strength: Patterns appear once the dish is shaken a bit harder than gravity; at 1.7 million shakes a second the crests throw off droplets a few micrometres across.

effects.title: Coagulation
effects.effect: a pinch of salt makes fine particles clump together and sink
effects.description: A pinch of a salt like alum makes the fine particles clouding muddy water clump together and sink, leaving it clear. Hans Schulze showed in 1882 that the salt's electric charge decides how little is needed. Every waterworks does this.
effects.strength: A few milligrams of alum per litre clears muddy water in under an hour.

effects.title: Fluidization
effects.effect: gas blown up through a granular bed makes it flow like a liquid
effects.description: Blow air up through a bed of sand or powder and at a certain speed the grains lift apart and the whole bed starts behaving like a boiling liquid: you can stir it, pour it, and things float or sink in it. Fritz Winkler used it in Germany in 1922 to turn powdered coal into gas. Fluidized beds now crack crude oil into gasoline and burn coal and waste cleanly.
usedIn: Fluid catalytic cracking in oil refineries (1942)
Fluidized-bed dryers for food and medicines
effects.strength: A gentle updraft of a few centimetres per second is enough; a ball heavier than the sand sinks and a lighter one bobs up.

effects.title: Fluorescence
effects.effect: a material absorbs light of one colour and instantly gives off light of a longer, redder colour
effects.description: Some materials soak up invisible ultraviolet light and instantly give it back as visible colour, so they seem to glow under a black light. George Stokes worked it out in 1852 with quinine water, and named it after the mineral fluorite. It lights fluorescent tubes, makes highlighter ink and whitened laundry glow, and lets biologists tag cells with glowing proteins.
usedIn: Highlighter pens and optical brighteners in laundry detergent
Fluorescence microscopy with green fluorescent protein
effects.strength: The glow lasts only billionths of a second after the light goes off; a fluorescent tube gives about four times the light per watt of a filament bulb.

effects.title: Flutter
effects.effect: a flexible structure in moving air or water feeds on the flow and swings harder and harder
effects.description: Above a certain speed, a wing, tail, flag or bridge deck in moving air starts to twist and flap, each swing feeding the next, until it shakes itself apart. Frederick Lanchester traced the tail of a Handley Page bomber violently shaking in 1916 to this feedback. Engineers test every new aircraft against it, and wind-harvesters turn a fluttering ribbon into electricity.
usedIn: Flight flutter testing of new aircraft
Bridge-deck design after the Tacoma Narrows collapse (1940)
effects.strength: Below the critical speed nothing happens; just above it, swings grow in seconds, and the Tacoma Narrows Bridge tore apart in a 64 km/h wind.

effects.title: Free surface effect
effects.effect: loose liquid in a tilting vessel runs to the low side and tips it further
effects.description: Liquid sloshing in a half-empty tank, or grain shifting in a ship's hold, runs to whichever side the ship leans and tips it further. It has capsized ferries, but naval engineers also turn it around: a tuned tank of water that sloshes out of step with the waves calms a ship's roll.
usedIn: Baffles in road tankers and aircraft fuel tanks
effects.strength: Strong: water a few centimetres deep spread across its car deck was enough to capsize the ferry Herald of Free Enterprise in under two minutes in 1987.

effects.title: Frequency doubling
effects.effect: intense light passing through certain crystals partly comes out at double the frequency
effects.description: Shine a very intense laser through certain crystals and some of the light comes out at exactly half the wavelength, so invisible infrared turns into green light. Peter Franken's team found it in 1961 by focusing a ruby laser into quartz, just a year after the laser was invented. Green laser pointers make their light this way from an infrared laser, and microscopes use it to image collagen without dyes.
usedIn: Green laser pointers (1064 nm infrared doubled to 532 nm)
Green and ultraviolet lasers for eye surgery and chip inspection
Second-harmonic microscopy of collagen and muscle
effects.strength: Franken's first try converted about one part in a hundred million; modern crystals convert more than half of a strong pulsed laser beam.

effects.title: Friction
effects.effect: surfaces in contact resist sliding with a force proportional to how hard they press together
effects.description: Push a box across the floor and the floor pushes back. Amontons found the drag is proportional to how hard the surfaces press together, and oddly doesn't depend on how big the contact area is. Friction is what lets shoes grip, brakes stop cars and matches light.
effects.strength: Rubber on a dry road grips with a force up to about its own load (coefficient ~0.7-1); steel on ice manages only about 0.03.

effects.title: Grain-boundary strengthening
effects.effect: smaller crystal grains make a metal stronger
effects.description: Metal made of smaller crystal grains is stronger, because the boundaries between grains block the slipping that lets metal bend. Eric Hall (1951) and Norman Petch (1953) worked out the rule; steelmakers now roll and cool steel carefully to keep the grains tiny.
usedIn: High-strength low-alloy steel in car bodies
effects.strength: Shrinking the grains from about 0.1 mm to 0.01 mm roughly doubles the strength of mild steel, without adding any alloy.

effects.title: Ground effect
effects.effect: a wing close to the ground gets more lift and less drag
effects.description: A wing flying closer to the ground or water than about half its span gets extra lift and less drag, because the surface stops air from escaping downward and swirling round the wingtips. Carl Wieselsberger measured it in 1922; pilots feel it as a 'float' just before touchdown.
usedIn: Soviet ekranoplans such as the 'Caspian Sea Monster'
effects.strength: Flying at a tenth of its span above the surface, a wing loses roughly half its induced drag, which is why ekranoplans could carry heavy loads on little fuel.

effects.title: Hall effect
effects.effect: a magnetic field pushes current to one side of a conductor, creating a sideways voltage
effects.description: Run a current through a thin strip in a magnetic field and a small voltage appears across the strip's sides, because the field pushes the moving charges toward one edge. Edwin Hall found it in 1879 as a graduate student at Johns Hopkins. It lets a chip sense a magnet without touching it.
usedIn: Hall sensors timing brushless motors in fans and drones
Lid-closed sensors in laptops and phones
effects.strength: Microvolts in a metal, but in a semiconductor chip a fridge magnet gives millivolts, plenty to detect position or current.

effects.title: Helmholtz resonance
effects.effect: air in a cavity with a narrow neck rings at one note
effects.description: Blow across the mouth of an empty bottle and it hums: the air in the neck bounces like a weight on the springy air inside. Hermann von Helmholtz built tuned glass spheres on this principle to pick single tones out of music, published in 1863.
usedIn: Car intake and exhaust resonators that cancel drone
Tuned sound absorbers in concert halls
effects.strength: A wine bottle hums at roughly 100-200 Hz; a tuned box can soak up one low note almost completely while letting others pass.

effects.title: Hot chocolate effect
effects.effect: a few bubbles in a liquid slow sound in it dramatically
effects.description: Tap a mug while stirring in cocoa powder and the note drops sharply, then slowly climbs back as the froth clears: tiny air bubbles make the liquid springy and slow sound down enormously. Physicist Frank Crawford described it in 1982.
usedIn: Bubble curtains that muffle offshore pile-driving noise to protect porpoises
US Navy 'Prairie-Masker' air systems that hide ship noise
effects.strength: Just 1% air bubbles cuts the speed of sound in water from about 1,500 m/s to roughly 120 m/s.

effects.title: Hydraulic jump
effects.effect: a fast shallow stream abruptly jumps up into a deep slow one, churning away its energy
effects.description: When a fast, shallow stream suddenly slows, its surface leaps up in a standing step of churning water; you can see one as the ring around where a tap's stream hits the sink. Giorgio Bidone first studied it by experiment in Turin around 1819. Engineers build one in on purpose at the foot of dams to burn off the water's destructive energy.
usedIn: Rapid mixing of chemicals at water-treatment plants
effects.strength: A jump in a spillway basin can destroy well over half the energy of water falling tens of metres, within a few tens of metres of concrete.

effects.title: Hygroscopy
effects.effect: some substances pull water out of the air
effects.description: Some substances pull water vapour out of the air and hold on to it; certain salts take up so much that they dissolve into a puddle of their own brine. It's why salt cakes in a damp shaker, and why a sachet of silica gel keeps a shoebox dry.
usedIn: Calcium chloride spread on dirt roads to keep dust down and on icy roads
Honey and jam stay unspoilt partly because sugar pulls water out of microbes
effects.strength: Calcium chloride can soak up more than its own weight in water from humid air.

effects.title: Iridescence
effects.effect: thin transparent layers reflect different colours at different angles
effects.description: Some surfaces change colour as you tilt them, like soap bubbles, peacock feathers and CDs, because stacked thin layers make light waves reinforce one colour at one angle and another at the next. Robert Hooke looked at peacock feathers under his microscope in 1665 and traced the colours to thin layers, not pigment.
usedIn: Holographic foil on cards and packaging
effects.strength: Layers a few hundred nanometres thick, about 1/200 of a hair, give brilliant colours that never fade because no dye is involved.

effects.title: Johnsen-Rahbek effect
effects.effect: a voltage makes a metal and a semiconducting surface cling tightly together
effects.description: Put a voltage between a metal plate and a slightly conductive stone or ceramic touching it, and the two cling far harder than ordinary static would allow, because charge piles up across the tiny gaps where they touch. Danish engineers Alfred Johnsen and Knud Rahbek reported it in 1923 and built relays and loudspeakers on it.
usedIn: Electrostatic chucks holding silicon wafers in chip fabs
effects.strength: A few hundred volts gives a grip of a few kilopascals, enough to hold a wafer flat, many times the pull of plain static at that voltage.

effects.title: Joule heating
effects.effect: electric current heats the wire it flows through
effects.description: Current flowing through a wire heats it, in proportion to the wire's resistance and the square of the current, so doubling the current gives four times the heat. James Joule measured it in 1841, before his famous work on the mechanical equivalent of heat.
usedIn: Fuses that melt to cut a circuit
effects.strength: A kettle's coil turns 2-3 kilowatts into heat, boiling a litre of water in about two to three minutes.

effects.title: Kármán vortex street
effects.effect: flow past a cylinder sheds swirls from alternate sides, shaking it at a steady rate
effects.description: Wind flowing past a pole or wire peels off swirls alternately from each side, leaving a zigzag trail and shaking the pole side to side; it's what makes power lines sing. Theodore von Kármán explained the pattern in 1911 at Göttingen.
usedIn: Spiral strakes on chimneys and car antennas that stop shaking
effects.strength: Swirls come off at about one-fifth of the wind speed divided by the width: a 10 m/s wind past a 1 cm wire gives a 200 Hz hum.

effects.title: Kelvin-Helmholtz instability
effects.effect: a boundary between two fluids sliding past each other rolls up into waves
effects.description: When one layer of fluid slides over another, such as wind over water, the boundary rolls up into a row of curling waves; it's why some clouds look like a line of breaking surf. Helmholtz described it in 1868 and Lord Kelvin in 1871.
usedIn: Shear-layer mixing in jet-engine combustors and chemical mixers
effects.strength: Any speed difference across a sharp boundary sets it growing; on a calm sea it takes a moderate breeze to raise waves this way.

effects.title: Kerr effect
effects.effect: an electric field makes a clear material change the polarization of light
effects.description: An electric field makes some clear liquids and glasses split light like a polarizing crystal, so between two polarizers they can switch a beam on and off in under a billionth of a second. John Kerr found it in glass in Glasgow in 1875.
usedIn: Kerr-cell shutters in high-speed photography and early television
effects.strength: Weak: a centimetre-long cell of nitrobenzene needs tens of thousands of volts to switch fully, but responds in under a nanosecond.

effects.title: Lagrangian points
effects.effect: a small body stays put relative to two big orbiting bodies at five balance points
effects.description: Around any two orbiting bodies, like the Sun and Earth, there are five spots where a small object's pulls balance so it keeps pace with them. Joseph-Louis Lagrange found them in 1772 in Berlin (Euler had found three). Space telescopes park there for a steady view with little fuel.
usedIn: James Webb Space Telescope at Sun-Earth L2
effects.strength: Sun-Earth L1 and L2 lie 1.5 million km from Earth; a craft there needs only a few metres per second of thrust a year to stay.

effects.title: Laminar flow
effects.effect: slow or narrow flows move in smooth layers instead of churning
effects.description: Slow or narrow flows slide along in smooth, parallel layers; speed them up and they break into churning eddies. Osborne Reynolds showed in 1883, with a thread of dye in a glass pipe, that a single number predicts which you get. Smooth flow means far less drag and clean, predictable streams.
effects.strength: Water in a 1 cm pipe stays smooth below about 20 cm/s; keeping air laminar over a wing cuts skin drag there several-fold.

effects.title: Leidenfrost effect
effects.effect: a liquid on a surface far above its boiling point floats on a cushion of its own vapour
effects.description: Flick water onto a very hot pan and the drops skate around for a minute instead of hissing away: the bottom of each drop boils into a thin cushion of steam that holds it up and insulates it. Johann Gottlob Leidenfrost described it in 1756.
usedIn: Cooks' water-drop test for a hot pan
Boiler and nuclear-reactor tube design (avoiding film boiling)
Quenching steel, where the steam blanket slows cooling
effects.strength: Above about 200 °C a water drop hovers on a steam layer a tenth of a millimetre thick and lasts over a minute; at 150 °C it would be gone in seconds.

effects.title: Liquid crystals
effects.effect: a liquid whose lined-up molecules can be turned by a voltage to block or pass light
effects.description: Some substances flow like a liquid yet keep their rod-shaped molecules lined up like a crystal, so a small voltage can swing them round and change how light passes. Friedrich Reinitzer noticed in Prague in 1888 that a compound from carrots melted twice, first to a cloudy liquid, then to a clear one.
usedIn: Liquid-crystal displays in phones, TVs and watches
Liquid-crystal thermometer strips and mood rings
effects.strength: A few volts across a layer a few thousandths of a millimetre thick turns a pixel from clear to dark in milliseconds.

effects.title: Lotus effect
effects.effect: a surface of tiny waxy bumps makes water bead up and roll off, carrying dirt
effects.description: Water on a lotus leaf beads into near-perfect balls that roll off at the slightest tilt, picking up dirt as they go, because the leaf is covered in tiny waxy bumps that let drops touch almost nothing. Botanist Wilhelm Barthlott worked out how it keeps the leaf clean using electron microscopes, publishing with Christoph Neinhuis in 1997.
effects.strength: Drops sit with a contact angle above 150° and roll off when the leaf tilts by only a few degrees.

effects.title: Lubrication
effects.effect: a moving surface drags oil into a wedge-shaped gap and floats on it
effects.description: A spinning shaft drags oil into the narrowing gap of its bearing and builds enough pressure to float on it, so metal never touches metal. Beauchamp Tower discovered that pressure in 1883 when oil spurted from a hole drilled in a railway-axle bearing, and Osborne Reynolds explained it in 1886.
usedIn: Journal bearings in car engines and turbines
Michell thrust bearings on ship propeller shafts
effects.strength: An oil film thinner than a hair can carry tens of atmospheres of pressure and cuts friction to about a thousandth of the load.

effects.title: Magnetic hysteresis
effects.effect: a magnetic material keeps some magnetism after the field is removed
effects.description: Iron remembers: magnetise it and switch the field off and some magnetism stays, and to undo it you must push the other way; push hard enough and it stops responding at all (saturation). Emil Warburg measured this loop in 1880 and James Ewing, working in Japan, named it hysteresis a few years later.
effects.strength: A neodymium magnet resists being unmagnetised by fields of about a tesla, while soft transformer iron flips with a field tens of thousands of times weaker.

effects.title: Magnetocaloric effect
effects.effect: a material heats up when magnetised and cools when the field is removed
effects.description: Some metals warm up when put in a strong magnetic field and cool when it's taken away, because the field lines up their atoms' tiny magnets and squeezes out heat. Pierre Weiss and Auguste Piccard described it in Zurich in 1917, and William Giauque used it in 1933 to get within a fraction of a degree of absolute zero.
usedIn: Adiabatic demagnetisation refrigerators on X-ray satellites such as XRISM
Prototype gas-free magnetic fridges using gadolinium
effects.strength: Gadolinium warms about 2-3 °C per tesla, so a strong permanent magnet heats it only a few degrees, but the cycle can repeat many times a second with no gas.

effects.title: Magnetohydrodynamics
effects.effect: a magnetic field pushes on a current-carrying fluid, pumping it with no moving parts
effects.description: A magnetic field pushes on electric current flowing through a liquid like seawater or molten metal, so you can pump or steer it with no moving parts; and a conducting fluid flowing through a field makes electricity. Faraday tried to measure the Thames this way in 1832, and Hannes Alfvén founded the science in 1942.
usedIn: Yamato 1, a ship driven by seawater thrusters (1992)
Electromagnetic pumps for liquid sodium in fast reactors
effects.strength: Weak in seawater: Yamato 1 needed 4-tesla superconducting magnets to crawl at about 15 km/h, but it pumps molten metal easily.

effects.title: Magnetoresistance
effects.effect: a magnetic field changes a metal's electrical resistance
effects.description: A magnetic field changes how easily current flows through a metal; in iron and nickel the change depends on the angle between field and current. Lord Kelvin found it in 1856, and thin-film versions became the read heads of hard disks.
usedIn: Hard-disk read heads (anisotropic, then giant magnetoresistance)
effects.strength: Iron-nickel films change resistance by only a few per cent; the layered 'giant' version found in 1988 changes it by tens of per cent.

effects.title: Magnetostriction
effects.effect: a magnetic material changes shape when magnetised, and its magnetism changes when it is strained
effects.description: Iron gets very slightly longer or shorter when magnetised, so an alternating field makes it buzz: that is the hum of a transformer. James Joule measured it in 1842; the reverse also works, as stretching or twisting a magnetised rod changes its magnetism, which lets it sense force.
usedIn: Magnetoelastic torque sensors in e-bikes and power steering
effects.strength: Iron changes length by only about 20 parts per million; the alloy Terfenol-D by about 2,000 (2 mm per metre), pushing with great force.

effects.title: Magnus effect
effects.effect: a spinning object moving through air is pushed sideways
effects.description: A spinning ball moving through air curves sideways, because its spin drags the air faster past one side than the other. It's why a sliced ball swerves, and it drove ships with tall spinning cylinders for sails.
usedIn: Rotor ships (Flettner, 1924) and today's rotor sails on cargo ships
effects.strength: Strong enough to help push a cargo ship: modern rotor sails cut fuel use by roughly 5 to 20 percent.

effects.title: Marangoni effect
effects.effect: a liquid surface flows from low toward high surface tension
effects.description: Liquid flows from where its surface tension is low toward where it is high, dragging the surface along: a drop of soap sends pepper racing to a dish's edge, and wine climbs a glass in 'tears'. James Thomson explained the tears in 1855 and Carlo Marangoni studied the effect in 1865.
usedIn: Marangoni drying of silicon wafers with alcohol vapour
effects.strength: A trace of soap clears pepper across a dish in a fraction of a second; surface flows reach centimetres per second.

effects.title: Metal fatigue
effects.effect: a material weakened by repeated loading cracks below its normal breaking strength
effects.description: A metal part bent back and forth many times cracks and breaks under loads far below what would snap it in one go. Wilhelm Albert, a German mining official, first documented it in iron hoist chains in 1837, and August Wöhler's railway-axle tests in the 1860s showed the limits. It's why you can snap a paperclip by bending it, and why airliners are rated for a set number of flights.
usedIn: Wöhler fatigue testing of railway axles
Airliner fatigue-life rules after the de Havilland Comet crashes (1954)
Snapping wire or paperclips by bending without tools
effects.strength: Steel can break after about a million cycles at half the load that would snap it at once.

effects.title: Mirage
effects.effect: light bends as it passes through air of changing temperature, shifting images
effects.description: Over hot ground the air near the surface is thinner, so light skimming it bends upward and you see a shimmering 'pool' that is really the sky. Gaspard Monge explained it in 1798 while in Egypt with Napoleon's army.
usedIn: Photothermal-deflection ('mirage') spectroscopy for measuring faint absorption in coatings
Gradient-index (GRIN) lenses in endoscopes and fibre connectors
Schlieren imaging of shock waves and air flows
effects.strength: The bending is only a fraction of a degree, but over a few hundred metres of hot road it shifts the image by metres.

effects.title: Moiré effect
effects.effect: two overlaid fine patterns make broad bands that magnify any small shift between them
effects.description: Lay one fine grid or striped screen over another at a slight angle and broad wavy bands appear that neither pattern has, sweeping across when one layer moves a hair. Lord Rayleigh pointed out in 1874 that these bands could test how evenly a diffraction grating was ruled. Because the bands magnify tiny shifts, they are used to measure small movements and strains and to make banknotes hard to copy.
usedIn: Moiré fringe gratings in machine-tool position encoders
Moiré strain measurement on bridges and machine parts
Anti-copy line patterns on banknotes and ID cards
Moiré alignment marks in chip lithography
effects.strength: Two gratings with lines 0.1 mm apart crossed at 1 degree make bands about 6 mm wide, so a shift between them is magnified about 50 times.

effects.title: Negative refraction
effects.effect: a wave entering a specially structured material bends backward to the same side it came from
effects.description: In specially built materials a light or radio wave bends the 'wrong' way at the surface, ending up on the same side of the perpendicular it came from, so a flat slab can focus like a lens. Victor Veselago predicted it in 1967, and David Smith's team first showed it with microwaves in 2000 using a metamaterial made of tiny copper rings and wires. It drives work on 'superlenses' that see finer detail than ordinary lenses and on cloaks that steer waves around objects.
usedIn: Superlens experiments imaging details finer than the wavelength
Flat metamaterial lenses for microwave and radar antennas
Research cloaks that steer microwaves around an object
effects.strength: Works well for microwaves in lab metamaterials; for visible light it is still weak and lossy, absorbing most of the light within a few wavelengths.

effects.title: Negative thermal expansion
effects.effect: a material that shrinks when it's heated
effects.description: Some materials shrink when heated: zirconium tungstate contracts steadily from near absolute zero to 700 °C. Mixed into other materials it cancels out their swelling, for mirrors and fillings that keep their shape.
usedIn: Zero-expansion glass-ceramic cooktops and telescope mirrors
Mounts for optical-fibre sensors that must not drift
effects.strength: Zirconium tungstate shrinks by about a third as much as aluminium grows, enough to cancel out the swelling of whatever it's mixed into.

effects.title: Nucleation
effects.effect: a new bubble, droplet or crystal starts only on a tiny seed or rough spot
effects.description: Bubbles, droplets and crystals don't form evenly through a liquid or gas; they start on a speck, a scratch or a seed, which is why soda fizzes from the same spots on a glass. John Aitken showed around 1880 that water vapour won't form fog droplets without dust specks to start on. Supplying the right seeds makes rain, crystals or bubbles appear on command, from cloud seeding to click-to-start hand warmers.
usedIn: Cloud chambers, where droplets form on particle tracks
Reusable sodium acetate hand warmers triggered by clicking a metal disc
effects.strength: Without any specks, air must hold several times its normal limit of water vapour before droplets form; one seed can set a whole pouch of supercooled solution crystallising in seconds.

effects.title: Ostwald ripening
effects.effect: small crystals or droplets shrink and feed their material to larger neighbours
effects.description: In a mix of small and large crystals or droplets, the small ones slowly dissolve and their material builds onto the big ones, so the mix gets coarser over time. Wilhelm Ostwald described it in 1896. It is why ice cream turns gritty after weeks in the freezer, and chemists use it on purpose to grow crystals big enough to filter or to make fast photographic film.
usedIn: 'Digesting' precipitates so they can be filtered in chemical analysis
Physical ripening of silver halide grains in photographic emulsions
Ice-cream stabilisers designed to slow it
Controlling particle size in nanoparticle and catalyst making
effects.strength: Slow but steady: ice crystals in stored ice cream grow from about 0.03 mm to over 0.05 mm in a few weeks, big enough to feel on the tongue.

effects.title: Ouzo effect
effects.effect: adding water to an oil dissolved in alcohol makes the oil burst into a stable cloud of tiny droplets
effects.description: Pour water into clear ouzo or absinthe and it instantly turns milky: the anise oil, dissolved in the alcohol, comes out as countless tiny droplets that stay suspended without any shaking. Stephen Vitale and Joseph Katz studied and named it in 2003. The same trick makes fine, stable emulsions with no mixing energy, and is used to make nanoparticles and drug capsules.
usedIn: Nanoprecipitation of polymer nanocapsules for drug delivery
The clouding ('louche') of ouzo, pastis and absinthe
Solvent-shifting to make pigment and nanoparticle dispersions
effects.strength: Droplets are about a thousandth of a millimetre across and can stay suspended for days without stirring.

effects.title: Pascal's law
effects.effect: pressure applied anywhere to a confined liquid is passed on undiminished everywhere
effects.description: Push on a liquid sealed in a container and the push spreads equally to every part of it, so a small piston pressing on oil can lift a car resting on a large one. Blaise Pascal worked it out around 1653 and imagined the hydraulic press; Joseph Bramah built a working one in 1795. Every hydraulic brake, jack, lift and digger arm runs on it.
effects.strength: A piston with 100 times the area gets 100 times the force: a 20 kg push on a hand jack can lift a 2-tonne car.

effects.title: Peltier effect
effects.effect: an electric current through a junction of two materials pumps heat from one side to the other
effects.description: Run a current through a junction of two different metals or semiconductors and one side gets cold while the other gets hot; reverse the current and they swap. Jean Peltier noticed it in 1834, thirteen years after Seebeck found the reverse effect. It is the solid-state cooler, with no moving parts or gas, inside plug-in picnic coolers, small wine fridges and laser temperature controllers.
usedIn: Temperature control of laser diodes in fibre-optic transmitters
Compact wine fridges and hotel minibars
effects.strength: A matchbook-sized module can pump about 50 watts and hold one face up to about 70°C colder than the other, but it uses several times more power than a fridge compressor for the same cooling.

effects.title: Penning effect
effects.effect: a trace of a second gas lets an electric discharge start at a much lower voltage
effects.description: A pinch of a second gas makes a gas-filled tube light up at a much lower voltage: neon with half a percent of argon strikes far more easily than pure neon. Frans Penning explained it in the late 1920s: energy stored in excited neon atoms is handed to argon atoms and knocks electrons off them. Neon indicator lamps, plasma TV panels and radiation counter tubes use such 'Penning mixtures'.
usedIn: Neon indicator lamps (neon with about 0.5% argon)
Neon-xenon fill in plasma TV panels
Gas mixtures in radiation detector tubes
effects.strength: A fraction of a percent of argon can cut the voltage needed to light a neon tube by a third or more.

effects.title: Phononic crystal
effects.effect: a regular array of objects blocks sound or vibration over a band of pitches
effects.description: A regular array of rods, holes or lumps spaced about one wavelength apart completely blocks sound or vibration over a band of pitches while letting others pass. Manvyr Kushwaha and colleagues worked out the theory in 1993, and in 1995 researchers found that a steel-tube sculpture in Madrid did exactly this to traffic noise. It is used for acoustic mirrors in phone radio filters and for vibration-proof mounts, and proposed for 'seismic shields' of buried pillars.
usedIn: Acoustic Bragg mirrors under radio filters in mobile phones
Eusebio Sempere's steel-tube sculpture in Madrid, the first observed sound barrier of this kind
Proposed seismic shields of buried pillars
effects.strength: A periodic slab a few wavelengths thick can cut sound in its blocked band by 20 decibels or more, to a hundredth of the power.

effects.title: Phosphorescence
effects.effect: a material stores absorbed light and slowly gives it back as a glow in the dark
effects.description: Some materials soak up light and keep glowing after the light goes off, slowly fading over minutes or hours. In 1602 Vincenzo Cascariolo, a Bologna shoemaker and alchemist, baked a stone that glowed in the dark after sitting in sunlight, the 'Bologna stone'. Glow-in-the-dark watch dials, power-free exit signs, toys and long-glow radar screens use it.
usedIn: Photoluminescent exit signs that need no power
Long-persistence phosphor screens in radar displays
effects.strength: Modern strontium aluminate pigment, charged by ten minutes of light, stays visible in the dark for up to about 10 hours, though dimly.

effects.title: Photoacoustic effect
effects.effect: flickering light absorbed by a material makes it give off sound
effects.description: Flicker a light on a material and it gives off sound at the flicker rate, because each flash heats it slightly and makes it swell and shrink. Alexander Graham Bell discovered this in 1880 while building his photophone, which sent speech on a beam of sunlight. Today pulsed lasers use it to 'hear' blood vessels and tumours inside the body and to sniff tiny amounts of gas.
usedIn: Photoacoustic imaging of blood vessels and tumours
Photoacoustic CO2 sensors for building ventilation
effects.strength: With sunlight it is a faint hum you need an ear tube to hear; with a pulsed laser it can detect a gas at a few parts per billion.

effects.title: Photochromism
effects.effect: light switches a material to a different colour, and it switches back in the dark
effects.description: Some substances change colour in bright light and change back in the dark, over and over. Carl Fritzsche reported in 1867 that an orange solution of tetracene bleached in daylight and regained its colour in the dark. It is what makes eyeglass lenses that darken outdoors and clear indoors.
usedIn: Self-darkening eyeglass lenses (Corning photochromic glass, 1964; Transitions lenses)
effects.strength: Eyeglass lenses go from clear to sunglass-dark, passing only about 15-20% of light, within a minute in sunshine, and take a few minutes to clear.

effects.title: Photoconductivity
effects.effect: a material conducts electricity much better when light falls on it
effects.description: Some materials, like selenium, let electricity through far more easily in light than in the dark. Willoughby Smith noticed in 1873 that the selenium resistors he used to test undersea telegraph cables gave readings that changed with the sunlight. Light meters, dusk-to-dawn streetlight switches, early TV cameras and the drum in every photocopier and laser printer use it.
usedIn: Photoconductive drums in photocopiers and laser printers
Cadmium sulfide sensors that switch streetlights on at dusk
effects.strength: A cheap cadmium sulfide cell drops from millions of ohms in darkness to a few hundred ohms in daylight, a thousandfold change.

effects.title: Photodissociation
effects.effect: light with enough energy breaks molecules into pieces
effects.description: Light with enough energy can snap molecules apart, which is why sunlight fades dyes and turns some silver salts black. Johann Heinrich Schulze found in 1717 that silver salts darkened where light hit them, not where heat did, the effect photography later built on. High in the sky, ultraviolet light splitting oxygen molecules is what makes the ozone layer.
usedIn: UV lamps that make ozone for water treatment
Light-cured dental fillings and gel nails (photoinitiators)
effects.strength: Mostly needs ultraviolet or blue light; each photon breaks at most one bond, so it is slow in daylight but fast under a strong UV lamp.

effects.title: Photophoresis
effects.effect: light heating one side of a tiny particle in a gas pushes the particle along
effects.description: Tiny specks of dust or smoke drift along a strong light beam, or even against it, because the side the light heats pushes harder on the surrounding gas. Felix Ehrenhaft described it in 1918. Researchers use it to trap and steer single particles in mid-air, including a 2018 display that draws glowing 3D images with a laser-held speck.
usedIn: Sorting aerosol particles by how they absorb light
Proposed light-lofted micro-flyers in the upper atmosphere
effects.strength: Only works on specks smaller than about a hair's width, but there it can beat gravity and hold soot particles aloft.

effects.title: Piezoresistive effect
effects.effect: squeezing or stretching a material changes its electrical resistance
effects.description: Stretch or squeeze a wire or a chip of silicon and its electrical resistance changes, so measuring the resistance tells you the force. Lord Kelvin found it in metals in 1856, and in 1954 Charles Smith found it is many times stronger in silicon and germanium. Strain gauges in scales and bridges, car engine pressure sensors and airbag crash sensors use it.
usedIn: Metal-foil strain gauges in bathroom and truck scales
Silicon pressure sensors in car engines and blood-pressure monitors
effects.strength: In metal foil a stretch of one part in a thousand changes resistance by about 0.2%; in silicon the same stretch changes it by 10% or more.

effects.title: Plateau-Rayleigh instability
effects.effect: a thin stream of liquid breaks itself into a row of equal drops
effects.description: A thin stream of water from a tap doesn't stay a smooth thread: it wobbles and breaks into a row of drops, because surface tension pulls it into shapes with less surface. Joseph Plateau measured it in 1873 and Lord Rayleigh explained its timing in 1878. Vibrating the jet at the right pitch makes perfectly even drops, the basis of the inkjet printers that mark dates on cans.
usedIn: Continuous inkjet printers that print dates on cans and bottles
Making uniform droplets for capsules and beads
effects.strength: A stream breaks into drops spaced about 4.5 stream-widths apart, each roughly twice the stream's width; an inkjet nozzle makes over 60,000 drops a second this way.

effects.title: Pockels effect
effects.effect: an electric field changes how a crystal bends light
effects.description: An electric field changes how strongly certain crystals bend light, in step with the field. Crystals that switch light this way put data onto optical fibres and fire the pulses of many lasers.
usedIn: Pockels cells that switch laser pulses on and off
Modulators that put internet data onto fibre-optic light
effects.strength: Needs thousands of volts across a crystal, but switches light in under a billionth of a second.

effects.title: Poisson effect
effects.effect: a material squeezed in one direction swells in the other two
effects.description: Squash a rubber block from the top and it bulges out at the sides; stretch a rubber band and it gets thinner. Siméon Poisson put a number on this sideways swelling in 1829. Rubber seals and wall anchors grip tighter by bulging when squeezed, and cork makes good wine stoppers because it barely bulges at all.
usedIn: O-rings and rubber stoppers that seal tighter when compressed
Rubber expansion anchors (well nuts) that grip a hole when tightened
Cork wine stoppers, which hardly bulge
effects.strength: Rubber swells sideways by about half as much as it is squashed, steel by about 0.3 times, cork almost not at all.

effects.title: Precession
effects.effect: a sideways push on a spinning object's axis makes the axis swing around instead of tipping
effects.description: Push sideways on the axis of a spinning top or wheel and, instead of tipping over, the axis slowly swings around in a circle. Hipparchus saw it in the sky around 130 BCE as the slow drift of the stars, caused by Earth's tilted axis circling once every 26,000 years, and d'Alembert explained it with Newton's mechanics in 1749. Gyrocompasses, the self-steering of a leaning bicycle and MRI scanners, which read the precession of atomic nuclei, rely on it.
usedIn: MRI scanners, which detect precessing hydrogen nuclei
effects.strength: A fast toy gyroscope precesses about once a second; Earth's axis takes 26,000 years for one circle.

effects.title: Pyroelectric effect
effects.effect: a crystal produces a voltage when its temperature changes
effects.description: Some crystals, like tourmaline, become electrically charged at their ends whenever they are warmed or cooled. Theophrastus wrote around 314 BCE of a stone that attracted straw and ash when heated, and David Brewster named the effect in 1824. Motion-sensor lights and burglar alarms use it to feel the warmth of a passing person.
usedIn: Passive infrared (PIR) motion sensors in alarms and automatic lights
Flame detectors in industrial fire alarms
effects.strength: A pyroelectric sensor notices temperature changes of a thousandth of a degree, enough to sense a person's body heat 10 metres away.

effects.title: Pyrolysis
effects.effect: heating organic material without air breaks it into char, oil and gas
effects.description: Heat wood, coal or plastic strongly without letting air in and it doesn't burn: it breaks down into charcoal, tar, oil and burnable gas. People have made charcoal this way in covered pits and mounds for thousands of years. It makes coke for steelmaking and charcoal and biochar, made the coal gas that lit 19th-century cities, and turns waste plastic and tyres back into oil.
usedIn: Plastic and tyre recycling into fuel oil
effects.strength: Starts at around 400°C; a tonne of dry wood gives roughly 200-300 kg of charcoal.

effects.title: Pyrophoricity
effects.effect: a substance catches fire by itself on contact with air
effects.description: Some materials burst into flame by themselves the moment they touch air, usually finely powdered metals or very reactive chemicals. Scraping a hard cerium-iron alloy flings off tiny shavings that ignite instantly, the spark of a lighter flint; Carl Auer von Welsbach patented this ferrocerium in 1903. Rocket engines use pyrophoric liquids to light their fuel without a spark plug.
usedIn: Ferrocerium lighter flints and fire-starter rods
Triethylborane igniter in the SR-71's engines and SpaceX Merlin engines
effects.strength: Ferrocerium sparks burn at about 3,000°C, and triethylborane ignites in air even at -20°C.

effects.title: Radioluminescence
effects.effect: radiation hitting certain materials makes them flash or glow with light
effects.description: Some materials glow when struck by radiation from radioactive substances, each particle making a tiny flash of light. In 1903 William Crookes looked through a lens at a zinc sulfide screen near a speck of radium, saw it sparkle with countless separate flashes, and built the spinthariscope to show it. Tritium-lit watch hands and exit signs, and the scintillation counters that detect radiation, use it.
usedIn: Tritium-lit watch hands, gun sights and exit signs
Scintillation counters and hospital gamma cameras
Detectors in PET and CT scanners
effects.strength: Each alpha particle makes a flash just visible to dark-adapted eyes; a tritium exit sign glows with no power for 10-20 years, but only bright enough to see in the dark.

effects.title: Rayleigh scattering
effects.effect: particles much smaller than the light's wavelength scatter blue light far more than red
effects.description: Air molecules scatter blue light far more than red, so the sky looks blue in every direction and the setting sun, whose light has lost its blue on the long way through the air, looks red. John Tyndall saw blue light scattered by fine haze in the 1860s, and Lord Rayleigh worked out in 1871 that the shorter the wavelength, the much stronger the scattering. It sets how clear optical fibres can be and lets lasers measure the air high above.
usedIn: Rayleigh lidar that measures upper-air temperature
Light-scattering instruments that weigh polymer molecules
Explains the blue sky and red sunsets
effects.strength: Blue light is scattered about five times more than red; in the best glass fibre it still costs half the light every 20 km or so.

effects.title: Rayleigh-Taylor instability
effects.effect: a heavy fluid resting on a lighter one breaks into growing fingers and plumes
effects.description: When a heavy fluid sits on a light one, or a light fluid pushes on a heavy one, the boundary can't stay flat: it grows fingers and mushroom shapes that sink and rise into each other. Lord Rayleigh worked it out in 1883 and G. I. Taylor extended it in 1950 to accelerating fluids. It is why water spills from an upside-down glass even though air pressure could hold it up, why big explosions make mushroom clouds, and the main thing laser-fusion fuel capsules must be designed to resist.
usedIn: Fuel-capsule design for laser fusion at the National Ignition Facility
Rising wax blobs in lava lamps
Simulations of supernovas and mushroom clouds
effects.strength: Fast: ripples on the surface of water held upside down grow and spill in a fraction of a second; in a fusion capsule tiny ripples grow a thousandfold in billionths of a second.

effects.title: Resonance
effects.effect: small pushes at an object's natural rhythm build up into very large vibrations
effects.description: Push a swing in time with its own rhythm and each small push adds up until it flies high; anything that can vibrate, from a wine glass to a bridge to an electric circuit, responds hugely to pushes at its own natural frequency and hardly at all to others. Galileo described it in 1638, noting that well-timed puffs of breath could set a heavy pendulum swinging. Radios tune to one station this way, quartz watches keep time by it, and MRI scanners use it to pick out hydrogen atoms.
usedIn: Tuned circuits that select one station in radios
Tuned mass dampers that steady skyscrapers such as Taipei 101
effects.strength: A good quartz crystal or tuning fork builds its swing up thousands of times over from tiny pushes; a singer matching a wine glass's pitch can shatter it.

effects.title: Shape-memory alloy
effects.effect: a bent metal returns to its remembered shape when heated
effects.description: A bent wire of nickel-titanium snaps back to its original shape when warmed, as if it remembered it. Buehler's team at the US Naval Ordnance Laboratory found it in their alloy Nitinol, and it now opens heart stents inside arteries and shuts off scalding shower water on its own.
effects.strength: A nitinol wire as thin as a pencil lead can lift a few kilograms as it shrinks back by about 4 percent when warmed.

effects.title: Shear thickening
effects.effect: a liquid turns stiff when it is pushed or hit quickly
effects.description: Some mixtures, like cornstarch stirred into water, pour like cream when handled gently but turn hard the instant they are struck or pushed fast. Reynolds described the related swelling of packed grains (dilatancy) in 1885, and the effect now stiffens impact pads the moment they are hit.
usedIn: D3O impact pads in sports gear and phone cases
Speed bumps that stay soft for slow cars
effects.strength: A pool of cornstarch and water holds a person running across it, but they sink if they stand still.

effects.title: Skin effect
effects.effect: fast-alternating current flows only in a conductor's outer skin
effects.description: Fast alternating current crowds into the outer skin of a wire, the more so the faster it alternates. That's why radio aerials can be hollow tubes, and why induction furnaces harden only the surface of steel.
usedIn: Induction hardening of gears and shafts
Braided Litz wire in chargers and radios
Hollow copper tubes in radio transmitters
effects.strength: At mains frequency the current keeps to the outer centimetre of copper; at radio frequencies, to a fraction of a millimetre.

effects.title: Sputtering
effects.effect: fast ions knock atoms off a surface so they coat nearby objects
effects.description: Charged gas atoms slammed into a metal plate knock atoms loose, which then settle as a thin, even coating on anything nearby. Grove noticed metal from the cathode of a glow discharge tube coating the glass in 1852; today it lays down the films on hard disks, microchips and energy-saving window glass.
effects.strength: Each incoming ion knocks off roughly one atom, so coatings grow slowly, a few nanometres per second, but are extremely even.

effects.title: Stick-slip
effects.effect: sliding surfaces jerk in a repeating cycle of gripping and slipping
effects.description: Two surfaces grip, then suddenly slip, then grip again, many times a second, because gripping friction is stronger than sliding friction. It's what makes a violin bow sing and a door hinge squeak, and engineers now use it to inch tiny motors along by nanometres.
usedIn: Violin and cello bows with rosin
Stick-slip piezo motors in nanopositioning stages
effects.strength: A bowed violin string sticks and slips hundreds of times a second (440 times for the A string), loud enough to fill a concert hall.

effects.title: Stokes drift
effects.effect: passing waves slowly push floating things forward
effects.description: Waves don't just bob floating objects up and down: each wave carries them a little further forward than back, so they slowly drift in the direction the waves travel. Stokes worked this out in 1847, and it's used to forecast where oil slicks, debris and people lost at sea will drift.
effects.strength: Under ordinary sea waves the drift is a few centimetres per second, enough to carry a floating object a few kilometres a day.

effects.title: Stroboscopic effect
effects.effect: flashing light makes fast repeating motion look frozen or slowed
effects.description: A spinning wheel lit by a flashing light seems to stand still, or creep slowly backwards, when the flashes keep pace with its turning. Plateau and Stampfer built spinning slotted discs around it in 1832, and mechanics still use it to read the speed of engines and machines without touching them.
usedIn: Timing lights for setting car engine ignition
effects.strength: A strobe flashing a few thousand times a minute can freeze a fan or engine part spinning at the same speed so it can be read like a still picture.

effects.title: Supercooling
effects.effect: a liquid cooled below its freezing point stays liquid until disturbed
effects.description: Very clean, still water can be cooled well below freezing and stay liquid, then turn to ice in a flash when shaken or seeded. Fahrenheit saw it in sealed bulbs of water in 1724; dropping dry ice into supercooled clouds later became cloud seeding, and supercooling now keeps donor organs alive longer without freezing them.
