effects.strength: A bottle of purified water can sit liquid in a freezer at minus 10 degrees and turn to slush in seconds when tapped; tiny droplets stay liquid down to about minus 40.

effects.title: Superelasticity
effects.effect: an alloy bent far out of shape springs fully back as its crystals change form and change back
effects.description: Certain alloys, above all nickel-titanium, can be bent or stretched far more than ordinary metal and spring right back, because the strain flips their crystals into another arrangement that flips back when let go. Arne Ölander first saw such rubbery behaviour in a gold-cadmium alloy in 1932; nickel-titanium ('Nitinol') came from the US Naval Ordnance Laboratory in 1962. It is used in eyeglass frames you can twist, orthodontic wires and artery stents.
effects.strength: Nitinol springs back from about 8% stretch, roughly ten times more than spring steel.

effects.title: Superheating
effects.effect: a liquid heated past its boiling point stays liquid until disturbed
effects.description: Water heated in a very clean, smooth container can rise above its boiling point without boiling, then erupt all at once when disturbed. Donny heated air-free water far past 100 degrees in the 1840s; Glaser later used a superheated liquid to make the bubble chamber, where passing particles leave trails of bubbles.
usedIn: Boiling chips and stones that prevent bumping in labs
effects.strength: Water in a smooth mug can pass 100 degrees in a microwave and erupt when a spoon goes in; air-free water has been held liquid above 130 degrees.

effects.title: Superhydrophilicity
effects.inventor: Rong Wang, Kazuhito Hashimoto and Akira Fujishima
effects.effect: light makes a coated surface so water-loving that water spreads flat
effects.description: Glass coated with titanium dioxide and left in sunlight makes water spread into a thin, clear sheet instead of beading into drops. A Tokyo team reported it in 1997, and it gives self-cleaning windows that rinse off in the rain and car mirrors that never fog.
effects.strength: After an hour or so of sunlight, water spreads to an almost perfectly flat film, so rain sheets dirt off a window instead of leaving spots.

effects.title: Superplasticity
effects.effect: a hot metal stretches to many times its length without breaking
effects.description: Some fine-grained alloys, when hot, can be stretched like toffee to many times their length without snapping. Pearson pulled a tin-bismuth strip to nearly 20 times its length in 1934, and factories now blow hot sheets of such alloys into moulds like glass to make aircraft and car body panels.
usedIn: Car body panels for low-volume sports cars
Hollow titanium fan blades in jet engines
effects.strength: Pearson's strip stretched almost twenty-fold; ordinary metals snap after stretching less than half their length.

effects.title: Supersaturation
effects.effect: a liquid holds more dissolved than it should until a seed sets it off
effects.description: A hot liquid can dissolve extra salt or sugar and keep it dissolved as it cools, until a speck or a jolt makes it all crystallise at once. Lowitz studied these overloaded solutions and seeding them with a crystal in the 1790s; the same trick makes clickable hand warmers and, in air, the cloud trails of the cloud chamber.
usedIn: Cloud chambers for seeing particle tracks
effects.strength: Clicking the metal disc in a hand warmer crystallises the whole pack in seconds and warms it to about 54 degrees.

effects.title: Surface acoustic wave
effects.effect: sound travels as a ripple along the surface of a solid
effects.description: Sound can run along the skin of a solid like a ripple on a pond, staying near the surface instead of going through. Rayleigh predicted these waves in 1885 to explain earthquake shaking; ripples on piezoelectric chips now filter radio signals in every mobile phone.
usedIn: SAW radio filters in mobile phones
effects.strength: On a chip the ripples are only a few atoms tall and travel at about 3 kilometres per second, but they can sort radio channels precisely and even push droplets around.

effects.title: Surface tension
effects.effect: the surface of a liquid pulls tight like a stretched skin
effects.description: A liquid's surface behaves like a stretched skin, pulling drops round and holding up light objects. Young explained it, and how it sets whether a liquid wets a surface, in 1805; it shapes the droplets fired by inkjet printers, and soaps work by weakening it so water can soak into cloth.
usedIn: Shot towers dropping molten lead into round shot
effects.strength: Water's skin holds up a dry steel needle or a pond skater, a pull of about 0.07 newtons along each metre of edge.

effects.title: Surfactant action
effects.effect: molecules with a water-loving end and an oil-loving end let oil mix into water
effects.description: Soap and detergent molecules have one end that loves water and one that loves oil, so they line up at the edge between the two and let grease be carried away in water. Irving Langmuir showed in 1917 how these molecules stand on end at a surface. It's how soap cleans, and it lets oil and water mix in mayonnaise and paint.
usedIn: Lung surfactant drugs for premature babies
effects.strength: A few drops of washing-up liquid in a sink of water is enough to lift the grease off a pile of plates.

effects.title: Synchrotron radiation
effects.inventor: Frank Elder, Anatole Gurewitsch, Robert Langmuir and Herbert Pollock
effects.effect: fast electrons bent by magnets give off intense light and X-rays
effects.description: Electrons whirled around a ring at nearly the speed of light throw off a brilliant beam of light and X-rays as they turn. A General Electric team saw the glow through the glass of their synchrotron in 1947; giant rings are now built just to make this light for imaging proteins, materials and engine parts.
usedIn: Synchrotron light sources for protein crystallography
effects.strength: A synchrotron beam is billions of times brighter than a hospital X-ray tube.

effects.title: Thermoacoustic effect
effects.effect: heat makes a tube of gas sing, and sound can pump heat
effects.description: Heat one end of a narrow tube and the air inside starts to sing; run it backwards and loud sound inside a tube pumps heat from one end to the other. Glassblowers heard their hot bulbs hum, Sondhauss studied it in 1850, and engineers now build fridges and engines with no moving parts on it.
usedIn: Thermoacoustic freezer prototype built for Ben & Jerry's
Preventing combustion instability in rocket engines
effects.strength: A heated test tube can hum loudly, and laboratory thermoacoustic engines turn heat into hundreds of watts of sound power.

effects.title: Thermochromism
effects.effect: a material changes colour with temperature
effects.description: Some dyes and crystals change colour as they warm or cool, so a surface can show its temperature at a glance. It's what makes mood rings and colour-changing mugs shift, and what reads a child's fever on a strip pressed to the forehead.
effects.strength: The colour shifts over a span of just a few degrees, enough to read body temperature to about half a degree.

effects.title: Thermoluminescence
effects.effect: a heated crystal glows with energy stored from past radiation
effects.description: Some crystals that have soaked up radiation glow faintly when warmed, releasing the stored energy as light. Boyle saw a diamond glow when he held it against his skin in 1663; the glow now dates ancient pottery and measures the radiation dose on workers' badges.
usedIn: Thermoluminescence dating of pottery and burnt flint
Checking whether food has been irradiated
effects.strength: The glow is usually too faint to see without a sensitive light detector, but it grows in proportion to dose, so it can record thousands of years of background radiation.

effects.title: Thermophoresis
effects.effect: small particles drift from hot regions toward cold ones
effects.description: Tiny particles drift away from hot surfaces toward cold ones, pushed by the harder knocks of hotter gas molecules on one side. Tyndall saw a dust-free zone above a hot rod in a beam of light in 1870; it's why walls darken above radiators, and it's used to catch smoke for sampling and to build up the glass inside optical fibres.
usedIn: Thermal precipitators for sampling dust and smoke
effects.strength: The push is gentle, far weaker than a light breeze, but next to a hot wire it keeps a layer of air about a millimetre thick completely clear of smoke.

effects.title: Thixotropy
effects.effect: a gel thins when stirred and thickens again at rest
effects.description: Some thick gels turn runny when shaken or stirred and slowly set again when left alone. Schalek and Szegvári found iron-oxide gels doing this in 1923; it's why non-drip paint brushes on smoothly yet stays put on a wall, and why drilling mud holds rock chips up when the pumps stop.
effects.strength: Non-drip paint thick enough to stand on a vertical wall thins under a brush in a second and stiffens again within a minute.

effects.title: Total internal reflection
effects.effect: light hitting a surface at a shallow angle from inside is fully reflected
effects.description: Light inside glass or water that hits the surface at a low enough angle is reflected back completely, as if the surface were a perfect mirror. Kepler described it in 1611; it keeps light trapped inside optical fibres for kilometres and folds the light path in binocular prisms.
effects.strength: It reflects essentially 100 percent of the light, better than any silver mirror, once the angle passes about 42 degrees in glass.

effects.title: Townsend discharge
effects.effect: one free electron in a gas multiplies into an avalanche of charge
effects.description: In a gas under a strong voltage, one stray electron knocks loose others, which knock loose more, until a whole avalanche of charge rushes across. Townsend worked out this chain reaction around 1897, and it lets a Geiger counter turn the passage of one particle into a loud click.
usedIn: Proportional counters and wire chambers in particle detectors
effects.strength: A single electron can multiply into a million or more within a millimetre of travel, in less than a microsecond.

effects.title: Mechanoluminescence
effects.effect: some solids give off light when crushed, rubbed or strained
effects.description: Some crystals flash light when they're crushed, scratched or pulled apart: crunch a lump of sugar in the dark and it sparks blue. Francis Bacon described the sugar sparks in 1605. Coatings that glow where they're strained can show cracks in bridges and wings.
usedIn: Stress-sensing paints and films (still mostly in labs)
Peeling sticky tape in a vacuum gives off enough X-rays to image a finger (2008)
effects.strength: Faint: you need a dark room to see most of it.

effects.title: Turbulence
effects.effect: a smooth flow breaks into chaotic swirling eddies above a certain speed
effects.description: Past a certain speed, a smooth flowing stream breaks into chaotic swirls that mix everything in it. Reynolds showed the switch by running a thread of dye through a glass pipe in 1883; dimples on a golf ball use it to fly twice as far, and engines use it to mix fuel and air.
usedIn: Swirl chambers for mixing fuel in engines
effects.strength: Water in a garden-hose-sized pipe turns turbulent above about a quarter of a metre per second, slower than walking pace.

effects.title: Tyndall effect
effects.effect: small particles in a liquid or gas scatter a light beam so it shows
effects.description: A beam of light shining through smoke, fog or milky water becomes visible from the side because tiny particles scatter it. Tyndall studied it in 1869; it let Zsigmondy's ultramicroscope see particles too small for ordinary microscopes, and it's how many smoke alarms sense smoke.
effects.strength: Even a faint haze makes a beam visible from the side; it's why headlight beams show up in fog.

effects.title: Ultrasonic capillary effect
effects.effect: ultrasound drives a liquid far higher up narrow channels
effects.description: Strong ultrasound makes a liquid climb far higher and faster up a thin tube or into fine pores than it normally would, driven by bubbles collapsing at the tube's mouth. Konovalov reported it in 1961, and it's used to drive liquids deep into porous parts and narrow gaps.
usedIn: Ultrasonic impregnation of porous castings and coil windings
effects.strength: Under strong ultrasound a liquid rises in a fine tube several times higher than by capillary action alone.

effects.title: Viscoelasticity
effects.effect: a material springs back slowly and flows a little under load
effects.description: Some materials act partly like a spring and partly like thick honey: they spring back slowly, sag under a steady load, and soak up shocks. Weber noticed silk threads in his instruments slowly creeping under load in 1835; the effect makes memory foam hold your shape and foam earplugs expand slowly to fill the ear.
effects.strength: Memory foam takes a few seconds to recover its shape; Silly Putty bounces like a ball but flattens into a puddle over an hour.

effects.title: Vortex ring
effects.effect: a puff of fluid rolls into a spinning ring that travels far without spreading
effects.description: A sharp puff of air or water rolls up into a spinning doughnut that holds together and travels far, like a smoke ring. Helmholtz showed in 1858 why such rings keep spinning, and toy air cannons use them to knock over cups across a room.
usedIn: Vortex-ring guns tested for crowd control
effects.strength: A ring puffed from a bucket-sized box can cross a room, 10 metres or more, and still blow out a candle.

effects.title: Vortex cooling
effects.effect: whirling compressed air splits into a hot stream and a cold stream
effects.description: Compressed air whirled inside a tube splits into a hot stream out one end and a cold stream out the other, with no moving parts. Factories use vortex tubes to cool cutting tools and electrical cabinets.
usedIn: Cooling for electrical cabinets in hot factories
effects.strength: Chills compressed air from room temperature to about −40 °C, but wastes a lot of compressed air doing it.

effects.title: Water hammer
effects.effect: a moving liquid stopped suddenly sends a sharp pressure spike along its pipe
effects.description: Shut a tap suddenly on fast-flowing water and the pipes bang, because the moving water slams to a stop and sends a pressure spike racing back through the pipe. Nikolai Zhukovsky worked out its size in 1898 after Moscow's water mains kept bursting. The hydraulic ram pump harnesses those bangs to lift water uphill with no motor at all.
effects.strength: Stopping water moving at 1 metre per second all at once raises the pressure by about 14 atmospheres.

effects.title: Wiegand effect
effects.effect: a treated wire flips its magnetism suddenly and gives a sharp pulse
effects.description: A specially twisted wire flips its magnetism all at once as a magnet passes, giving off a sharp electric pulse no matter how slowly the magnet moves. Wiegand patented the wire in the 1970s, and it powers battery-free rotation counters and the classic Wiegand access-card readers.
usedIn: Pulse counters in water and gas meters
effects.strength: Each flip gives a pulse of a few volts in a small coil, enough to power a counter chip for an instant with no battery.

gap.effect: black stripes soak up light, white gaps reflect it
gap.how: Reads a price at the checkout in a blink. A laser spot sweeps across printed stripes, and a photocell turns the flicker of reflected light, strong from the white gaps and weak from the black bars, into a number the computer looks up.
gap.name: Barcode scanner
gap.revision: Narrower effect (r11): black bars soak up light while white gaps reflect it. Borderline: it may really be an improvement.

gap.effect: catalysis
gap.how: The box in a car's exhaust that removes most of its poisons. Hot exhaust passes over a ceramic honeycomb coated with platinum, which speeds up the reactions that turn carbon monoxide, unburned fuel and nitrogen oxides into carbon dioxide, water and nitrogen, without being used up itself.
gap.name: Catalytic converter

gap.effect: photoelectric effect
gap.how: The chip that replaced film in cameras and telescopes. Light falling on each pixel knocks electrons loose, so the brighter the spot the more charge collects; the charges are then shuffled out row by row and counted.
gap.name: CCD image sensor

gap.effect: nerve signals are electrical
gap.how: Gives hearing to people who are profoundly deaf. A microphone and chip split sound into pitches, and a row of electrodes threaded into the inner ear gives tiny shocks to the hearing nerve at the right places, which the brain learns to hear as sound.
gap.name: Cochlear implant

gap.effect: a rolling ball grips the surface instead of sliding
gap.how: A pointer you move by hand. A rubber ball underneath grips the desk and rolls rather than slides, turning two small wheels at right angles, so the computer can count how far the hand moved left-right and up-down.
gap.name: Computer mouse
gap.revision: Narrower effect (r11): the ball grips and rolls instead of sliding.

gap.effect: parts of a mixture travel at different speeds
gap.how: Reads the letters of a gene, and later of the whole human genome. Copies of the DNA are made that stop at each letter, and the pieces are pulled through a gel, where shorter ones travel faster, so their order spells out the sequence.
gap.name: DNA sequencing

gap.effect: static charge
gap.how: The working memory of every computer. Each bit is a small electric charge parked on a microscopic capacitor next to a transistor switch. The charge leaks away, so the chip tops it up thousands of times a second.
gap.name: Memory chip (DRAM)

gap.effect: atoms are tiny magnets
gap.how: A computer's long-term memory. A head floating a hair's width above a spinning platter flips the direction of tiny magnetized patches, one bit each, and they keep their direction with the power off.
gap.name: Hard disk drive

gap.effect: compressed gas pushes back
gap.how: A craft that travels over water, mud, sand or ice alike. A fan blows air under the hull, where a rubber skirt holds it in; the trapped air is squeezed and pushes back hard enough to lift the craft off the surface, so there is almost no friction.
gap.name: Hovercraft

gap.effect: currents stirred up inside a metal heat it
gap.how: A stove top that heats the pan but not itself. A coil under the glass makes a rapidly changing magnetic field, which stirs up swirling currents inside the iron pan, and the pan's own resistance turns them into heat.
gap.name: Induction cooktop
gap.revision: Narrower effect (r11): currents stirred up inside the pan heat it, not just 'induction', which the transformer already has.

gap.effect: piezoelectricity
gap.how: The everyday home printer. Behind each of hundreds of tiny nozzles a crystal flexes when given a voltage and squirts out a droplet of ink, thousands of times a second, while motors step the head across the page and feed the paper.
gap.name: Inkjet printer
gap.revision: Added electric motors for moving the head and paper (Boris's note).

gap.effect: lined-up rod-like molecules make a fibre as strong as its bonds
gap.effectCardNew: Some substances flow like a liquid while their long molecules stay lined up like a crystal; an electric field or a flow can swing them all round together.
gap.how: The fibre in bulletproof vests, five times stronger than steel for its weight. Its molecules are stiff rods that line up by themselves in a liquid-crystal solution, and spinning the solution into a fibre freezes them in line, so a pull is taken by the strong bonds along every molecule.
gap.name: Kevlar
gap.revision: Proposes a new card, Liquid crystals (1888), shared with the LCD. The way it works is confirmed.

gap.effect: signal delay gives distance
gap.how: Measures distance by timing light, from surveyors' tools to the distance to the Moon. A laser fires a short pulse, a photocell catches its reflection, and since light's speed is known exactly, the round-trip time gives the distance, to within centimetres even off mirrors left on the Moon.
gap.name: Laser rangefinder

gap.effect: lined-up liquid crystals twist light, and a voltage untwists them
gap.effectCardNew: Some substances flow like a liquid while their long molecules stay lined up like a crystal; an electric field or a flow can swing them all round together.
gap.how: The flat screen of watches, laptops and TVs. A film of liquid crystal sits between two crossed polarizing sheets; its molecules twist the light so it gets through, and a small voltage straightens them so that dot goes dark.
gap.name: Liquid crystal display
gap.revision: Proposes a new card, Liquid crystals (1888), shared with Kevlar.

gap.effect: water molecules soak up microwaves and heat up
gap.how: Heats food in a minute or two. A magnetron fills the box with microwaves, which water molecules soak up by jiggling back and forth billions of times a second, so the food heats from the inside while the plate stays cool.
gap.name: Microwave oven
gap.revision: Narrower effect (r11): water soaking up microwaves, not just 'radio waves', which the magnetron already has.

gap.effect: atomic nuclei in a magnet answer radio waves
gap.how: Takes detailed pictures of soft tissue like the brain, with no radiation. In a very strong magnet the hydrogen nuclei in the body's water all line up; a radio pulse tips them over, they ring back with faint radio signals, and a computer works out where each signal came from.
gap.name: MRI scanner

gap.effect: small molecules seep through a membrane
gap.how: How most of the world's desalination plants make drinking water from the sea. A thin plastic membrane lets water molecules through but not salt; normally water would flow toward the salty side, but pushing the sea water hard enough forces it the other way.
gap.name: Reverse-osmosis desalination

gap.effect: radiation ionizes what it passes through
gap.how: The cheap ceiling alarm found in most homes. A speck of radioactive americium knocks electrons off air molecules, so a small current flows across a gap; smoke particles soak up the charged molecules, the current drops, and the alarm sounds.
gap.name: Ionization smoke detector

gap.effect: some metals lose all resistance when very cold
gap.how: The powerful magnets inside MRI scanners and particle accelerators. Coils of special wire, cooled by liquid helium to a few degrees above absolute zero, lose all electrical resistance, so they carry enormous currents with no heat and no power once started.
gap.name: Superconducting magnet

gap.effect: heat radiates as invisible light
gap.how: Sees people, animals and hot engines in total darkness or smoke, used by firefighters and soldiers. Everything warm gives off infrared light, the warmer the brighter; a special lens and sensor chip turn that invisible glow into a picture.
gap.name: Thermal imaging camera

gap.effect: static charge
gap.how: A screen you point at with a finger, as on every phone. A grid of transparent electrodes under the glass holds a small charge; a fingertip, which conducts, draws some of it away, and the chip finds the spot where the charge dropped.
gap.name: Capacitive touchscreen

gap.effect: sound echoes off the boundaries between soft tissues
gap.how: Lets doctors see inside the body without X-rays, most famously the unborn child. A probe sends pulses of very high-pitched sound and listens for the faint echoes from every boundary between organs; the timing of each echo places it on a screen.
gap.name: Ultrasound scanner
gap.revision: Narrower effect (r11): echoes off the boundaries between soft tissues.

gap.effect: atoms are tiny magnets
gap.how: A tape recorder fast enough for television. A spinning electromagnet head lines up the tiny atomic magnets in a coated plastic tape, so the picture is kept as a trail of magnetized spots that can be played back the same evening.
gap.name: Video tape recorder

future.effect: pollen fertilizes a flower to make seed

effects.effect: pollen fertilizes a flower to make seed

future.how: Bees are dying off, about a third of our food depends on pollinators, and indoor farms have no bees at all. Rather than a tiny flying robo-bee, which would need batteries far smaller and stronger than any we have, this is a full-size robot arm that rolls along greenhouse rows on mains power. Its camera finds open flowers and it dabs pollen from one onto another with a soft brush or puff of air, so each flower can set fruit without insects.
future.name: Pollinating robot
future.obstacle: Speed: a hive visits many thousands of flowers an hour while the arm takes seconds per flower, so it only pays off for valuable crops like tomatoes and strawberries.

future.effect: heating limestone frees a gas that lime soaks back up

effects.effect: heating limestone frees a gas that lime soaks back up

future.how: Solar power stops at night, and batteries big enough to cover it are costly. By day, concentrated sunlight bakes limestone, driving off carbon dioxide, and the lime and the gas are kept in separate tanks, which can hold the energy for months. At night the gas is let back onto the lime, which soaks it up and gets very hot, raising steam to spin a turbine; limestone is cheap and found almost everywhere.
future.name: Limestone battery
future.obstacle: Each bake-and-soak cycle makes the lime grains crack and crumble so they soak up less gas, and no plant has yet run for years at power-station size.

future.subtitle: a solar battery made of baked limestone
future.why: Black's 1750s lime experiment as a battery for solar power.

future.effect: two overlaid fine patterns make broad bands that magnify a small shift

effects.effect: two overlaid fine patterns make broad bands that magnify a small shift

future.how: About one in five breast-cancer survivors gets lymphedema, a lifelong arm swelling that is easiest to reverse in its first millimetres, yet it is checked with a tape measure at clinic visits. A stretchy band carries two overlapping fine-line prints; when the arm grows even a millimetre around, the lines shift and broad stripes slide visibly along the band (moiré), so the wearer sees the change every morning.
future.name: Moiré swelling band
future.obstacle: Telling real swelling apart from the band slipping or the arm being held differently.
future.real: Limb-swelling wearables use capacitive sleeves, strain bands or 3D bodysuits, and moire strain indicators exist for structures, but no moire band for limb circumference was found.
future.subtitle: an armband that shows early lymphedema
future.why: Free daily self-checks catch lymphedema while it can still be reversed.

future.how: Rockets spend most of their fuel just reaching orbital speed, which is why getting to space is costly. A cable of carbon nanotubes runs from a base at sea on the equator straight up, past the height where a satellite circles once a day, to a counterweight beyond it; the Earth's spin flings the counterweight outward and keeps the cable taut. Electric climbers, powered by sunlight or a laser beamed from the ground, ride up the cable carrying payloads to orbit at the cost of electricity.
future.name: Nanotube space elevator
future.obstacle: The cable must be about 100,000 km long and stronger for its weight than any material yet made in bulk; the longest nanotubes are centimetres. It must also survive lightning, debris and orbiting satellites.
future.real: Studied since Artsutanov (1960) and Clarke's 1979 novel; NASA and Obayashi have published designs and laser-powered climber contests have run, but no cable has been built.
future.ruleNote: Borderline: Rotating tethers are an old, sound idea that could cut launch costs, but the cable has never been made and reusable rockets are already lowering costs, so is it still worth chasing? My pick: keep.
future.subtitle: a cable to orbit that payloads climb
future.why: A space elevator would make reaching orbit cost about as much as the electricity to lift the payload.
